title: Tale of the Unjust King and the Tither

keywords: tale of the unjust king and the tither
full_text:
An oppressive King of ancient Yemen appointed an unscrupulous tax-collector named Kardan, with orders to collect a tithe of one-tenth of every harvest, herd, and catch of fish across the realm.

Kardan, seeking to enrich himself, increased the tithes to one-third, then one-half, seizing the milk-cows of farmers, the nets of fishermen, and the looms of weavers. Within three years, the farmers ceased to plow, the fishermen abandoned their boats, and the markets of Yemen were deserted.

Famine struck the capital, and the royal treasury ran dry.

One morning, an honest old farmer entered the royal audience hall carrying an empty wooden basket. He placed the basket before the throne and said:

'O King! Look upon this basket. Three years ago, it was filled with sweet figs, and your tither took two figs, leaving eighteen for my children; we ate, prospered, and planted ten new trees.

Last year, your tither took fifteen figs, leaving five; my children hungered, and we could not buy water.

This year, your tither came to seize all the figs, but finding my trees dead of drought, he cut down the wood for his hearth! Now my orchard is dead, your basket is empty, and both you and I must starve together!'

The words struck the King like an iron hammer. He looked at his empty treasury, looked at the ruined countryside, and realized that by destroying the producers, he had destroyed his own crown.

The King dismissed the greedy tither, abolished the oppressive taxes, and distributed free seeds from the royal granaries, learning that a kingdom flourishes only when its producers are allowed to thrive.
moral: Oppressive taxation that bleeds the productive laborer destroys the prosperity of the commonwealth.
